segments.text: Regulatory Authority, our Director General, thank you so much, sir. Ambassador Laura Holgate is with us. She is the President at LSHH International Advisors, but also former U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations.
Mr. Lars van Dassen is here with us. He is an Executive Director at WINS, which is the World Institute for Nuclear Security. And we wrap up the panel with Madam Sarah J.G. Lennon.
She is an International Nuclear Policy Advisor with Nano nuclear Energy. Thank you very much. Let's give them all a round of applause.
Thank you for making the time. And I'm going to try to the best of my ability to work our way through the panel. And Mr. Loyiso Tyabashe, I'm going to start off with you.

One of the things we've spoken about today to a large extent, especially in this moment, is that public mistrust is not just a social hurdle. This is not a social issue. It actually is a potential hurdle to delivery overall.

My question to you is, how do we build in trust by design as we're thinking about nuclear projects so that trust and public trust is not an afterthought, but really is designed into both the building of the project and the execution of the project? Thank you very much. I think this is at the core of everything that we do, especially when we try to deploy these projects. The first thing we need to do is for us to orientate ourselves, self-reflection as the nuclear industry, in that we are so good in talking about neutrons, electrons, protons, we forget what the public is all about.

So, once we identify that this is our social license to operate, that's when we'll change our orientation and take this even more seriously than we do today. So, for me, the first thing is that this is a social license to operate. It's not nice to have, it is an imperative, and we need to take it seriously.

And we also need to move from just pure communication to engagement, meaningful engagement, not just engagement. Because it is at that point when you start to realize the do's and the don'ts in whatever culture or society, the likes and the dislikes, the must-do's and must-not-do's. That becomes very important.

And it happens at a lower level in building trust, which is that understanding of where the other person comes from. And most importantly, we really need to build this in as an essential ingredient in the form of proactive communication. Like it was said earlier on, once a decision is made, it's way too late to start engaging people.

So, we need to take the communities, engage them as we move along, as we lead up to the decisions that need to be made. So for me, that's really, it sums everything up in that manner, in that let's be proactive, let's be meaningful, let's be deliberate in what we do, and we can be sure of the good results at the end. I think the language you bring into this conversation is excellent.
It is a social license to operate. You remind us that perhaps the change needs to start within. It's about a reorientation of the industry first before expecting change on the outside.

Let me build on that a little bit, Mr. Rugigana, by coming to you. Two of the young people in the audience asked important questions. One of those was, how do we actually measure transparency? And another one was, how do we actually make some of this information a lot more accessible? And the examples that was used was TikTok and Instagram.

And for me, I think the bigger question is, how do we make regulatory oversight a lot more understandable, accessible, and within reach of the ordinary citizens that make up communities? Thank you so much. Good afternoon, good evening. So from the previous session, we learned that electricity demand in Africa will continue to grow rapidly, and by 2040, 2050, it will double.

Currently, it's about 46%. In Rwanda alone, the growth is about, the demand is about 10% today. The good thing is we see countries in Africa positioning nuclear at the center of their medium to long-term strategies, energy strategies.

And for us, this is where we start from. Number one, so they have key pillars if you are to build trust, to be transparent, and also to ensure that everyone is involved. The first one starts with political leadership and commitment.

You saw since morning, even last year, African leaders are committed. They have this ownership, strong ownership, and this is very important to connect with our citizens. We also saw when you have this strong political commitment from our leaders, then it gives confidence to our citizens that there is long-term vision and direction of the country, and this builds trust and transparency among our citizens.

But at the same time, it promotes accountability, accountability, accountability, and of course, it helps us as regulators when they are totally fully committed, it helps us to build independent regulations, independent regulatory bodies. Now, back to your question, how do we make everything accessible? How do we connect with our ordinary citizens? The first one is we must have strong, independent regulatory bodies. That's number one.

This is, where do we get this? We must have, as Africans, and I will speak from practical experience from the regulatory perspective, that we must have, as Africa, good legislation that actually gives us this independence. In Rwanda, we have this, we have, that's why we have the Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Authority, we have Rwanda Atomic Energy Board, and as a regulator, we perform our duties independently from any government interventions or any pressure. So this separation of institutions is very key.

It gives us the power to engage with citizens, to make sure that when we are developing and designing these regulations, we consult them, they are getting involved in everything, and as we move towards developing our nuclear programs, and even the plants, we have to make sure that they are fully involved and consulted, the civil society, among others. Thank you. So let me be a little bit difficult, sir, because you raised three things which I think are quite important.

Political leadership and commitment. You talk about accountability, and you talk about independence, and I know Ambassador Holgate, you might have some thoughts on independence a little bit later, but I'm keen to not lose the response to one of the questions on the floor, which was, how do we measure transparency? How do we know that we're getting all the things that you've spoken about, how do we know that we're actually getting it right, that there is clarity at a community level with what is happening at a sub-regional, a national, or even at a municipal level? How do we know that we've got that transparency right? I think what we need to do is to make sure that what we do, the citizens are involved, the communities are involved. When they're involved, then there is transparency.

How do you involve communities? You have to make sure that in everything you do, in the regulations, the projects you want to implement, they are fully involved from initiation, implementation, to execution. I've got you. So there are many aspects around, but that is the summary.

Involve communities in everything that you do regarding a nuclear program. And of course, Mr. Roy Payne gave us some pathways in terms of how we actually involve communities, what are some of the underlying things we've got to be thinking about. Ambassador Holgate, let me bring you in because one of the things that's been clear today is that nuclear projects don't exist in isolation.
There's a much broader context that we've got to be thinking about. There are international standards, there are partnerships that go beyond national borders. There's geopolitics at play as well.

The question for you is, what do you make of the gap perhaps between global nuclear governance and the extent to which at a local level, we're trying to nurture and foster trust, and how do we close that gap a lot more intentionally so that whatever is transpiring at an international level has relevance and expression with what happens at a local level? Well, that's a really great question. And I think what we want to remember is that citizens really will want to know that nuclear energy projects proposed for their region are safe, that they're secure, and that they will be used exclusively for peaceful purposes. And the global standards for these attributes, which are generally accepted by everybody, are derived from treaties that nations negotiate and then choose to join, or sometimes not join.

Those are sovereign decision. There's also expert processes through which any member state can participate at the International Atomic Energy Agency and a number of other intergovernmental organizations that help take those treaty commitments and turn them into action. And so there's a lot of global participation in that.

And so when considering nuclear energy projects, citizens have a right to insist that these projects are consistent with the global standards that their government has agreed to abide by. And this is especially important given the global character of nuclear energy commerce. If international suppliers or even local firms are not integrating these standards into the design of the technology, it will be really more expensive for the local operators to manage those facilities over the 30, 50, 100-year lifetime of some of these institutions.

So the international standards can really help give comfort to communities that their governments are doing the right thing and that the companies involved are also doing the right thing. I think it links beautifully to the points that Mr. Rugegana made around if there are standards that the community can reference and they know that these apply globally, there is something against which we can hold our leaders and those project developers accountable against. And I think that's really helpful.

Let me then go to yourself, Mr. Pandasan, because as the Executive Director of the World Institute of Nuclear Security, I am keen to tap you to understand how do we talk about nuclear security and communicate about it in a way that doesn't automatically surface fear and cloud the conversation with fear. I'm reminded of the question raised by the young gentleman in the stands who his first entry into the conversation is, but what about Chernobyl? And I would imagine that there are similar narratives that we need to box our way through and navigate even as we have this conversation. Is it possible to do it without fear in the room? Thank you very much.

I think I will take the answer to a level where it's maybe not expected. But let me start by saying that there is a distinction between safety and security and where my organization is active, that is in the area of security. The issue that you raise, I have discussed with decision makers now over the past year in African states in six countries.

I think it's very important. If you raise the issue of nuclear security, there is immediately, well, that's a question of how high is the fence, have all the people been trained, et cetera, et cetera. But there's much more in it, and particularly in the context of Africa and African states.

And it is one where you have to think of, you have nuclear security, you should actually be thinking about nuclear and security. If you think of nuclear, then you go into which are the opportunities, which are the things that would be helpful for us. And there are lots of things that are not being discussed as very helpful.
Ultraviolet radiation of drinking water, I think that that would be fantastic. And it doesn't imply very many risks in terms of radiation. But there are many others.

But if we then look to the other side of the coin, security, there we also have to consider that we have to embrace and understand the full context. If you're in a country where it is that you have incursions from terrorist groups, et cetera, et cetera, that has to be taken very seriously. And if it is dealt with, that immediately bestows credibility upon the government.

This is where I think there is one thing that the two issues that have been raised during the day, but one is trust and another one is cooperation, but not much has been said about what kind of cooperation. And I think that there is one sleeping giant of cooperation opportunity in Africa that is not being considered, except that my organization has a big project with it. And that is the sub-regional cooperation that already exists in West Africa, ECOWAS, the Sahel Alliance, East African Community, SADC and for Central Africa as well, and for Northern Africa.

If it is, and here we reach the next crucial issue, and it is agency. A country that is seen and a government that is seen to seek and develop agency. So it means that it has its own decision power in terms of where it wants to go in the nuclear business.
That is a country that towards its people and constituency has that trust. Ultimately, that is what it's all about. And this is where I think, what it is we can achieve with agency.

If we would think of, for instance, 12 countries in ECOWAS, eight countries in East Africa, if they together develop what it is that they want and are able to go out and say what it is that they think is good for their country, energy development, et cetera, et cetera, then a lot is gained. Because there is a risk today that it's the other way around. That it is outside forces that come and say what it is that they think is helpful and would want to sell.
Thank you. I think those are incredibly helpful comments. And perhaps we might not even get the time to double-click on all of them, but I think very useful ingredients in the broader conversation.

I particularly like how you challenge us to think about not nuclear or security, nuclear and security, and how do we hold those in one conversation to interrogate what do we mean by cooperation and where does that cooperation sit? But I think the thing that most provokes me is this idea of decision-making sovereignty and how that is a critical ingredient to perceive trust or real trust at the very least. Madam Lennon, let me bring you into the conversation because we also know that there are new nuclear, a new entrance in the nuclear space as this opportunity is being focused on. We also know that we've got advanced reactor companies that are also coming into play.

My question is, are you seeing the opening up of these opportunities also coming with a re-imagining and a rethinking of public trust compared to traditional nuclear programs that we've seen around the world? Or is it more of the same? Well, thank you. I would say it's definitely not more of the same. I think we are in a very different place and we have learned from those who have gone before and what worked and what didn't work.

I think the idea now is that you need to engage the communities early and often. So this is echoing what some of my colleagues have mentioned, understanding that... Actually, let me just back up. I thought the questions that we got from the audience were absolutely spot on.

And the question about social media was something that I've been thinking about because there are organizations like Generation Atomic, which I think is looking to engage the younger generation and they are sort of meeting people where they are. And so developing manageable, accessible and accurate new information. And I think that's how we flip the script, as some might say.

And I think that's how you reach the younger generation. And that's what the new advanced reactor companies need to do and explain why the technologies that are being developed now, why the fuels are different from what was in Chernobyl. And the more you educate and explain at a very basic level, and I don't mean that in someone who is not smart, but in a very simple, non-technical way so you can understand this fuel is much safer than previous for these smaller reactors.

I'll say the company that I work for, Nano nuclear Energy, is a micro-reactor company. And we are planning to build our first reactor on a university campus within stone's throw of dormitories. So I think that kind of information really goes a long way to help develop that trust and say, this is safe.

This is not the fear-mongering reactors that there were before. And I think also the different priorities that the younger generation especially has now, we're talking about climate change, economic development, eliminating poverty or reducing, and all these benefits to going to the young gentleman's question about, how do you balance the two and what you were saying, explaining both the new benefits and the safety of the new advanced reactor designs and explaining why it is not risky. I think those and the benefits that will come for communities like I was talking about.

So I wanna just double click on something because I think you've really articulated so succinctly and this idea of it's not about explanation. It is about decoding and simplifying and that's how we make information more accessible, but also in line with the young lady who spoke earlier from the floor, meeting people where they're at. And I don't know how Mr. Roy Payne feels about this, but if they're on TikTok, that then answers the question, that's where they receive news and information from.
And so while it might have seemed far-fetched at the moment, actually maybe not so much after all. We've got just over 10 minutes left. So I'm going to do a lightning round of just final questions.

I wanna come back to you, Mr. Tyabashe . What's the hardest lesson you've learned about how public trust can quickly shift from an enabler to a derailer that you would like to share with the audience? And I suppose what I'm looking for is, what do we learn from that that we can all take away? So history is the best teacher and we tend to refuse to learn. And maybe just one example, theoretical, and then I'll come to the real example.

If you look at the history of the Eiffel Tower, which we all admire as the face of Paris, there was a huge protest in 1887 that it was a monstrosity, why would they bring it in the center of town? And that was a protest that people had valid reasons on, and these were mainly the artists. And today, no artist can draw Paris without an Eiffel Tower. So I think it's important to understand that you've overcome that state of winning public trust when people realize that they cannot live without what you have.

Just like we cannot live without our cell phones, we cannot live without the airplanes and automobiles today. That becomes important. But most importantly, in terms of the lessons that shift public trust to becoming a derailer, is in the project that I was involved in in my past life, where we were attempting to build a second nuclear power plant in South Africa, in the southern part of the country, is our stakeholder mapping was done so very well.

We knew what stakeholders to go to. We mapped, we even had the traditional leaders embedded in that, and we did approach, and people understood where we're at. Little did we know that there was also another sub element of the traditional people, which is seen as somewhat extinct in the country, but there's still smaller populations of it, the Koi.

And we really had a very big standing block because what they raised was they believe, not that they have, they believe they've got historical graves on our side. And how do you go about that? So that became a sudden change in the discussions in that amongst the conflicting and also the competing needs of the different community members, we found ourselves on our back foot. But it was good that we engaged and engaged with determination, trying to understand, and we managed to get to the bottom of the issue.
But very importantly, we need to listen and listen very carefully. Thank you very much. And so it's, again, a two-way communication and a two-way listening is what I'm hearing you say.

And one can imagine that emotional connection to that particular part of land would have been a massive stumbling block. Let me build on this again with you, Mr. Rugegana, because I can imagine that as a regulator, you're also looking at early warning flags and cautionaries. And to me, I think the best question is, what are the early warning signals one would need to look for in your nuclear project to ensure that it does not pose a delivery risk? How's the regulator thinking about these early warning mechanisms and broader systems? Thank you so much.

And my colleague talked about listening, listening, listening to the people. And this is, we need to start from there. But if you don't listen, then we are going to watch for TikTok, conference, the outcry.

So from the beginning, as I said and he has said, we need to involve everyone, we must listen, we must talk to people. So some of the, what we see, we go through this every day, the outcry on social media. We see a lot going on and whenever we launch a project and the citizens are not well involved, this is the feedback, the feedback.

Then we call for meetings, public meetings, consultative meetings and now few come, few stakeholders. That's a clear warning that there is a problem. And we see this in the projects we implement and the regulations we design.

Then we also go to, of course, petitions. When we look at many petitions from academic institutions, we receive them from civil society organizations, then you know that you need to be slow and listen to the people. And for any better policy regression, you must talk, engage and involve everyone from the beginning.

And if you don't do that, then you get it wrong. So for the successful implementation of any project, including nuclear, you must make sure that you map clearly very well all the stakeholders and then involve and consult with them. Then you have a better project and you deliver the result to the citizens.
Thank you. Sure. So what I'm hearing is that a quick stakeholder mapping is insufficient.

It is about the intentionality around the listening. It is about listening to unlikely sources. It would be interesting for me to see how many chief executives in the room have a TikTok account and are actually checking what the conversation on TikTok is about.

But what I'm also hearing you say is that when there's absence, to interrogate the absence and to try and understand who's not there and why are they staying away and not to dismiss petitions, especially if they come from smaller players, whether it's civil society or academia. I appreciate those inputs. I want to build on an earlier point you made as I go back to Ambassador Holgate.

Now, one of the things that Mr. Rugigana spoke about how independent oversight is an important way in which we hold ourselves accountable. And yet at the same time, we're talking about decision-making sovereignty. I think I've mentioned it at least once or twice today.

How do we balance the need for independent oversight and how that can lead to national credibility with the right balance of national control, which is also evidence of one of the ingredients that contributes to building trust? Yeah, well, every treaty that touches on nuclear safety, nuclear security, nuclear safeguards begins with a very strong statement that these are the responsibilities of the states' parties or of the member states. So there's no question that each country has a responsibility to uphold its international commitments on these topics. And the reality is that, as was mentioned by a couple of the questions even, safety and security failures can affect neighboring countries and indeed the whole global nuclear enterprise.

Look at how Chernobyl put a giant pause on nuclear power plant construction globally, a few decades later, did the same thing. So it's a responsibility, it's a right, but it's also a responsibility for each member state to make these decisions.

And so they really have to follow the best practices that have been derived and documented over 70 years of nuclear operations. And so this is the... And some of these include things like a transparent and independent regulator. And so that's been a standard recognition of the best practice across, ever since nuclear regulation came into being, that they can't be captured.

Now, what that means is independent from the industry, independent from who they're regulating, not independent from the government. And actually when I worked at the White House and I had to fight sometimes with our nuclear regulator on policy issues, I would remind them, you're still a government agency. Your independence has to do with the licensee.

And so that is, but it's still a really important principle. Others principles include security by design and also obviously the application of international safeguards through the International Atomic Energy Agency to confirm peaceful use. So these are commitments that have been undertaken and then member states have an ability through their own regulatory processes to put those into law, to put those into implementation, to put those into enforcement.
So what I'm hearing you say is that a balance is quite achievable. We just need to be very intentional around that. It's about the pursuit of best practice.
We know their best practice. I think you also have raised, Laura, that history has a lot to teach us. And so the best practice comes through.

I find it incredibly insightful, the distinction you make about who you are actually independent from? And I think sometimes we don't take the conversation to that level. Let me then come back to you, Mr. Van Darsen, because I had not left Johannesburg yesterday, anticipated that on a stage talking about nuclear energy, I'd end up talking about TikTok, but here I am. And this is where the conversation has led us.

I'm interested in hearing from you about the reality of the fact that we live in an era of misinformation as well. How do we make sure that we are really protecting both physical security and building public confidence at the same time in a world where misinformation is as part of the reality as anything else that we can touch at the same time? How do we separate and how do we create that distinction? It's an incredibly complicated question. I will try to rephrase it and make it a little simpler, but also be pinpointed exactly into the context we are in.

And this is about having your narrative right. If you have your narrative right, then you also create kind of a basis for what it is that can be discussed around it. And here comes one part of the narrative where it is that I think many things go astray.

One thing we have not heard so much about, and I've tried to count how many times I've heard climate change, decarbonization, and global warming. Global warming, I've not heard of it once. Decarbonization, I've heard once.

Climate change, I've heard twice. I actually think that that is very helpful because this is where the narratives also go in two directions. There is a Western narrative that climate change is very important.

It needs to be solved. But I've spent enough time here in Sub-Saharan Africa to know that their narrative is different and that it has to be different. Because if climate change is a problem, then it was not caused by Africa.
And it is not going to be, or it does not have to be solved by Africa. I'm really adamant in saying that. And I will also say why.

African vegetation and rainforests absorb three times more CO2 than is emitted here. If there would be a doubling of the production of electricity using natural gas in Africa, it would lead to an increase of CO2 emissions of 0.1%. So there's certain things in this we have to think about. And so the narrative in Africa has to be a different one.

That is, what will nuclear energy bring us in terms of electricity, but also the increase of knowledge, thousands of physicists, thousands of engineers, et cetera, et cetera, that then also venture into other areas. We've talked very little about the fact that now the SMR debate in Western countries, that is about SMRs and data centers. We need to be adamant that that is the same development here.
SMRs, production of electricity, also have data centers because that relates to economic development. And with that, political development. That has to be our focus.

And we have to look at it, we or them come from the outside. We have to try to see if there's a way we can see the world with the eyes of friends in Africa and try to understand that their first needs are different from the ones that are in the West. Thank you.

I don't think there's any more that I can say to underscore that point. I think it's exceptionally well-articulated from the applause in the room, well-received as well. Whose future are we re-imagining and from whose perspective are we doing it? As you can see, Sarah, we've got zero, zero, zero on the clock, but I am gonna sneak a final question to you just before we close.

I just want you to help us just leave here with clarity. There seems to be a view that smaller or advanced reactive designs inherently make trust building a lot more easier. True or false? And a quick response to that and then we'll close.

I would say that it's true. I think based on what my colleague here was just talking about, understanding the priorities of the area, the region, the countries that you're looking at, and understanding that a small modular reactor or a micro reactor can address those concerns, can alleviate those issues. I think the different solutions for different priorities is why the advanced reactors really have a good case and why that does make building the trust easier.

And I think also your question about transparency, I thought that was a really good question. If you afford me another moment or two. I think the question is about how do you know when you've reached transparency or how do you measure it? I think if you're engaging in community dialogue and repeating the efforts in talking to the communities, if you reach the point where you have answered all of the questions and you have shared the information, I think that's how you reach transparency.

Fantastic. I think it's a beautiful clause because you circle us back to the audience, which is where we wanted to start. Ladies and gentlemen, if I were designing the program, I would give at least another hour to this conversation because I think it is a critical conversation that is a make or break when it comes to translating ambition into action.
But here we are with powerful insights, with a panel of experts, and they've given us so very much.

parts.title: Roy Payne: How do we bridge the gap between reality and perception?

segments.text: Well, thank you, everybody. And I'm so pleased to be here. This is such an important debate, and it's so often not had.

So this conference is absolutely wonderful from my perspective. We've already heard today about de-risking nuclear projects and building long-term stability. And proactively managing public dialogue and engagement is a key tool in mitigating risk and laying the foundations for longer-term stability.

It therefore should be seen at the heart of project planning delivery, and not just as a communication program to which you sell your idea to a worried public after the decision has been made. Now, consent-based citing is often referred to as the gold standard in public dialogue. But what is consent-based citing? First, it's the polar opposite of the traditional DAD approach, decide, announce, defend, where public dialogue comes after decisions are made, and we tend to see the same outcomes every time, a delayed process, cost overruns, etc,...

Now, consent-based citing is not a fixed playbook, but an adaptable framework. Every country which has implemented consent-based citing has done so differently, according to its own political cultures and decision-making processes. But there are common principles which are evident in every consent-based citing process.

At the core of consent-based citing is an acceptance there will always be public anxiety and questions, and a distrust of government and the nuclear industry. Consent-based citing is about turning that inevitability to your project benefit, rather than let it be a risk with the proven potential to derail your project. Consent-based citing is not about selling your idea to the community.

It should never offer a community a simple binary choice. Yes, no, stop, go forward. It should always be an open, two-way dialogue that's not just a simple imparting of technical information, but a process to address the inevitable concerns that every community will have, and with the developer and the community together building a shared vision of the future they both seek.

Under consent-based citing, communities have to have agency and influence. Therefore, any consent-based citing process needs to provide communities with the capacities and the resources which allow them to meaningfully participate and collaborate in an equitable partnership. Co-designed local decision-making processes are highly effective.

How everyone will work together, how they resolve disagreements, how decisions will be made. This helps ensure that even if someone disagrees with a particular decision, they are more likely to accept that decision because they understand how and why it was made through a fair and transparent process which they helped design. I could go on, there's a lot more elements to consent-based citing, but I think we need to relate it today to the business and project benefits of taking a consent-based citing approach.

It allows you to use the early development and planning stages of a project constructively. If you integrate public dialogue and engagement at that stage, you can acquire early intel on potential issues and resolve many of them before they become a problem. Rather than develop your plan, consult the public afterwards, and then have to unwind that plan in response to their concerns and questions they raise.

Investing in and supporting the community's ability to participate meaningfully are actions which say more about you than your words. It's a key pillar of trust building, your actions and deeds rather than your words, and it shows that you're treating the community with respect. Building a relationship and developing a long-term shared vision with the community also provides for much more stable and sustainable project foundations that can last the lifecycle of the project.

Such stability obviously provides, well, should enhance investor confidence and mitigate against downstream cost escalations and project delays. And since the community will ask you questions anyway, allowing the community to openly vet information and find answers to their questions rather than just listen to your responses is the most cost-effective defence against miss and disinformation, because the very process of open investigation will also highlight the untruths perpetuated by project opponents. And communities and the public are not stupid.

They know when somebody is spinning them a yarn. So the evidence is clear. Early-stage investment in consent-based siting in terms of finance and of time reduces long-term costs and supports speedier project delivery dates.

And before I leave today, I just want to leave you with three thoughts to take forward as we look ahead from the issues raised in this conference. First one I want to talk about is trust. Trust is a two-way process.

And if industry and government wants the community to trust them, they will have to trust the community. And it's easy to view communities with suspicion, and even sometimes as adversaries, to be managed and maneuver around. But that tends to generate the very outcomes you're seeking to avoid, resistance against your proposals.

Consent-based siting provides the evidence that if communities are required to share the responsibility and be involved in decision-making, they generally act responsibly and in good faith. The second point I'd like to raise is about collaboration and joint learning between communities, and particularly between communities in different countries. The nuclear industry is a wonderful example of how humanity shares knowledge and learning.

But it shares it at a scientific, technical, safety, regulatory, legal, political, government level. The only level it doesn't provide that shared learning is at the community level, the people level. And yet it is at the community level that the nuclear sector often faces its greatest challenges.

And as Dr. Tamara said about trust, it's not necessarily the message, it's the messenger. People simply don't trust the nuclear sector or the government when they say something. Yet they might trust a friend or another community who's been through exactly the same experience.

Because the same issues and concerns are repeated in every community, in every country, and are re-litigated from scratch each time, which just brings confusion, cost, and delay on a repetitive basis. This and misinformation operates internationally. There is no comparable internationalized response mechanisms.

But allowing communities to learn directly from each other is the most powerful antidote to lack of trust and to managing this and misinformation. And I think this approach becomes even more important if African countries take a coordinated regional approach to developing nuclear infrastructure. You should also align and coordinate community learning across borders.
